question_text: In the metabolism of cytosine, what is one of the final products?

Explanation:

Cytosine is a pyrimidine base, and during its catabolism, it is first deaminated to uracil, which is then further broken down via the pyrimidine degradation pathway. question_text: A 10-month-old boy presents with recurrent oral lesions and respiratory infections. Laboratory investigations reveal reduced B cell, T cell, and NK cell counts along with reduced adenosine deaminase levels. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The most likely diagnosis based on the history of recurrent oral lesions and respiratory infections in an infant, along with reduced B cell, T cell, and NK cell counts and adenosine deaminase levels, is suggestive of severe combined immunodeficiency.

Severe combined immunodeficiency is a group of genetically diverse disorders with defects in both humoral and cell-mediated immunity.

Explanation of other options:

Agammaglobulinemia (Option A): Agammaglobulinemia is an X-linked recessive disorder and arises from mutations in the Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK) gene, which disrupts signalling from the pre-B cell receptor, leading to failure of B-cell precursors to mature into functional B cells and causing markedly reduced immunoglobulin levels. Clinically, the disorder manifests after about six months of age with recurrent bacterial respiratory infections, susceptibility to certain viral and protozoal infections, absence of plasma cells, underdeveloped lymphoid tissues, and normal T-cell function.

Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (Option B): Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by misfolded α1-antitrypsin protein, most often the PiZ variant, which accumulates in hepatocytes, leading to endoplasmic reticulum stress and impaired inhibition of neutrophil elastase, resulting in lung and liver damage. Clinically, it may manifest in infancy with severe liver disease progressing to cirrhosis, while pulmonary emphysema develops due to unchecked neutrophil elastase activity.

DiGeorge syndrome (Option C): DiGeorge syndrome arises from developmental failure of the thymus due to defects in the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches, most commonly linked to a 22q11 deletion involving the TBX1 gene. This results in deficient T-cell-mediated immunity, hypocalcemic tetany from absent parathyroids, and congenital malformations of the heart and great vessels, often accompanied by abnormal facial features. Clinically, patients show low T-cell counts, reduced resistance to fungal and viral infections, and depletion of T-cell zones in lymphoid organs, while immunoglobulin levels may be normal or reduced depending on the degree of T-cell deficiency.

question_text: Which of the following condition can lead to increased uric acid level in blood which is associated with reduced or absent uric acid in urine?
explanation:
Uric acid is an end product of purine nucleotide degradation. It is excreted by kidney. The daily excretion of uric acid is around 600 mg.

Normal level of uric acid in blood is 3 to 7 mg/dl in male & 2-6 mg/dl in females (lower in female compared to male)

Gout is a metabolic disorder that occurs due to hyperuricemia. Due to low solubility of uric acid in water, it will get deposited in the synovial joint, leading to arthritis.

Hyperuricemia is an increased level of uric acid in blood (more than 7mg/dl).

It may or may not be associated with increased excretion of uric acid in urine (uricosuria)

Option A: Defect in PRPP synthase enzyme:

Here PRPP enzyme activity is abnormally increased

It is involved in de novo synthesis of purine nucleotides. It is abnormally active, not subject to feedback inhibition by excess nucleotides. So increased purine synthesis, which is associated with increased uric acid excretion in urine also.

Option B: Lesch Nyhan syndrome occurs due to defect in HGPRT (Hypoxanthine guanine phosphoribosyl transferase) enzyme of purine salvage pathway.

If HGPRT is absent then it leads to,

  1. Accumulation of Hypoxanthine and guanine, which increased its catabolism
  2. Also decrease rate of salvage pathway, it results in accumulation of PRPP, which stimulate purine biosynthesis and later its catabolism

Both these will produce more uric acid and increased uric acid level, also increased uric acid excretion in urine

Option C: Leukemia is blood cancer, characterised by excessive cell turnover. So excessive nucleic acid is degraded into nucleotides and then to uric acid. So it will lead to overproduction of uric acid and hyperuricemia which is associated with increased uric acid excretion in urine

Option D: Lactic acidosis occurs due to accumulation of lactic acid in blood, then it excretes in urine. Lactic acid will compete with tubular secretion of uric acid, so reduced excretion of uric acid and increased uric acid level in blood.

Here hyperuricemia is not associated with increased uric acid level in urine.

Causes of Hyperuricemia & Gout– May be primary or secondary

I) Primary: Inborn error of metabolism which lead to overproduction of purines, which lead to increased purine catabolism, lead to overproduction of uric acids,

  1. Phosphoribosyl amido transferase (PRAT) enzyme activity increased
  2. PRPP synthase enzyme activity is increased Both enzymes are involved in de novo synthesis of purine nucleotides. They are abnormally active, not subject to feedback inhibition by excess nucleotides. So increased purine synthesis
  3. Deficiency of HGPRT and enzymes of salvage pathway: HGPRT is an enzyme in purine salvage pathway, so purine salvage reduced and increased purine nucleotide synthesis
  4. Deficiency of Glucose 6 Phosphatase (Von Gierk’s disease): Accumulation of glucose 6 phosphate (precursor of PRPP), which diverted to HMP shunt and increased ribose 5 phosphate which increased de novo synthesis.

II) Secondary: Secondary to other disorders, which lead to either over production of uric acid or reduced excretion of uric acid

A) Overproduction of Uric acid

  1. Malignancy which lead increased cell turnover, Polycythemia
  2. Treatment of malignancy: esp leukemia and lymphoma, leading to destruction of large amount of cell (acute tumor lysis syndrome)
  3. Alcohol consumption: increased production of ATP and breakdown of ATP
  4. Severe trauma due to damage to tissue
  5. Starvation due to increased rate of catabolism of tissue
  6. Psoriasis
  7. Increased dietary intake

B) Reduced excretion of Uric acid: Hyperuricemia is not associated with increased excretion of uric acid in urine (uricosuria)

  1. Impaired kidney function like renal failure will reduce excretion uric acid
  2. Metabolic acidosis either due to Lactic acidosis, Ketoacidosis etc will compete with tubular secretion of uric acid, so reduced excretion of uric acid
  3. Drugs like thiazide diuretics, loop diuretics etc - Inhibition of uric acid secretion by renal tubules

question_text: A frameshift mutation was introduced into the coding sequence of an mRNA. If this occurs at the 4th position in an mRNA with 900 nucleotides, which of the following is most likely to happen?
option_b: Partial loss of protein and function
option_c: Complete loss of protein and function
option_d: No change in function as it will be removed in post-translational modification
explanation:
Explanation:

The effect of a frameshift mutation occurring at the 4th position in an mRNA with 900 nucleotides would be the complete loss of protein and function.

  • Frameshift mutations occur when nucleotides are inserted or deleted from a gene in numbers not divisible by three, shifting the reading frame of mRNA and producing garbled protein sequences.
  • Such changes often result in nonsense codons, premature termination, or abnormal amino acid chains, though deletion or insertion in multiples of three simply removes or adds specific amino acids without altering the reading frame.
  • In the given scenario, since the frameshift mutation is occurring at a relatively earlier position, complete loss of protein and function is more likely. (Options A, B, and D ruled out)
  • Sometimes, a combination of insertions and deletions can restore the reading frame but still create partially abnormal proteins, a mechanism implicated in several human diseases.
  • The effects of insertions and deletions using a few examples are illustrated below.
  • Other types of mutations include single-base alterations, known as point mutations, which can be either transitions (a pyrimidine replaced by another pyrimidine or a purine by another purine) or transversions (a purine replaced by a pyrimidine or vice versa).
  • When such DNA changes occur in protein-coding regions, they are transcribed into mRNA, carrying the altered base to the corresponding site.
  • These mutations can have several effects: some may be silent, especially when occurring at the third codon position, where wobble reduces impact, resulting in no change to the protein.
  • Others may cause a missense mutation, leading to the substitution of one amino acid with another. Depending on the substitution, this may be harmless, partially disruptive, or completely detrimental to protein function.
  • In cases where the substitution is partially acceptable, the protein may retain some but abnormal activity, while unacceptable substitutions prevent normal functioning.
  • A more severe outcome occurs when the mutation introduces a nonsense codon, leading to premature termination of translation, producing truncated proteins that usually lack proper function.

question_text: A 55-year-old female presents with acute pain and erythema in her first metatarsophalangeal joint. Her serum uric acid is 9.4 mg/dL. She is prescribed a drug to lower uric acid levels. Inhibition of which enzyme is the primary mechanism of action of the most commonly prescribed drug for this purpose?
explanation:
Explanation:

In the given clinical scenario the female patient presented with symptoms and lab findings highly suggestive of Gout. The correct enzyme is Xanthine oxidase.

The first-line drug for chronic management of hyperuricemia is allopurinol (or its newer analog febuxostat), which works by inhibiting xanthine oxidase. This enzyme catalyzes the conversion of hypoxanthine to xanthine and xanthine to uric acid. Its inhibition reduces the production of uric acid.

Explanation of other options:

Phosphoribosyl transferase (HGPRT) (Option A): This enzyme is involved in the purine salvage pathway. A deficiency of HGPRT causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, which is characterized by hyperuricemia, but the drug allopurinol does not target this enzyme.

Thymidylate synthase (Option B): This enzyme is involved in the de novo synthesis of thymidine nucleotides (pyrimidine metabolism) and is a target for chemotherapeutic agents like 5-fluorouracil, not for gout treatment.

Dihydrofolate reductase (Option D): This enzyme is crucial for folate metabolism and is inhibited by drugs like methotrexate (used in rheumatoid arthritis) and trimethoprim. It is not involved in purine catabolism or uric acid production.

question_text: All tissue requires nucleotides for synthesis of nucleic acid and to meet their physiological demand. All of the following nucleotides are incorporated during synthesis of nucleic acid, except

explanation:
Nucleotide pools are used for synthesis of nucleic acid in human tissues. All tissue gets such nucleotides to meet their physiological demand by

  1. De novo synthesis mainly
  2. Salvage pathway (small amount)

Option A: Injected nucleotide compounds are seen to be incorporated in nucleic acid synthesis. So the incorporation of injected thymidine into newly synthesized DNA thus can be used to measure the rate of DNA synthesis.

Option B: Ingested (dietary) nucleic acids and nucleotides are considered as dietary nonessential, no dietary purine or pyrimidine is incorporated into tissue nucleic acids.

Following ingestion of nucleotide or nucleic acid in diet, their degradation results in mononucleotides, which may be absorbed or converted to purine and pyrimidine bases. The purine bases are then oxidized to uric acid, which may be absorbed and excreted in the urine.

Pyrimidine bases are degraded into CO2, NH3, beta alanine and beta aminoisobutyrate.

Option C: Nucleotides synthesized by de novo synthesis will serve as a major source of nucleotides during synthesis of nucleic acid in tissue. During de novo synthesis in tissue, purine or pyrimidine nucleotides are produced from various amphibolic intermediates.

Option D: Even nucleotides synthesized by salvage pathways, can also be used to synthesize nucleic acid in human tissue, in small amounts. In the salvage pathway, there is an addition of ribose phosphate to preformed purine or pyrimidine bases. Such purine or pyrimidine bases are derived from damaged DNA of broken down cells (recycled).

Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32nd edition CH 33 PN 328

question_text: Which of the following mechanisms explains how elevated homocysteine levels contribute to cardiovascular disease?
option_b: Enhanced platelet aggregation and endothelial dysfunction
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Homocysteine is an amino acid that is produced when the body metabolizes methionine. Normally, homocysteine is broken down by vitamins B6, B12, and folate.
  • Factors Leading to Elevated Homocysteine:
    • Vitamin B6, B12, and Folate Deficiency
    • Genetic Mutations: such as mutations in the MTHFR (methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase) gene, can lead to impaired homocysteine metabolism.
    • Chronic Diseases: Conditions like chronic kidney disease can increase homocysteine levels.
    • Lifestyle Factors: Smoking, alcohol consumption, and a high-protein diet may also elevate homocysteine.
  • Elevated homocysteine levels, a condition known as hyperhomocysteinemia, have been associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular diseases (CVD), such as coronary artery disease, stroke, and peripheral vascular disease. An elevated homocysteine levels contribute to cardiovascular disease by following mechanisms:
    • Endothelial Dysfunction
    • Thrombosis (Blood Clot Formation)
    • Increased Oxidative Stress
    • Promoting Atherosclerosis
    • Increased Vascular Stiffness
  • Proper intake of B-vitamins and managing other risk factors can help lower homocysteine levels and reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease.
  • Homocysteine has no effect on cholesterol production.(Option A)
    • Factors that increase cholesterol production & increase cholesterol level are diet, genetics, obesity, lack of physical activity, age and gender, medical conditions, excessive alcohol consumption & smoking, chronic stress
  • Homocysteine has no effect on blood pressure regulation and insulin signalling. (Option C & Option D)

Key take away

  • Homocysteine is an amino acid produced when the body metabolizes methionine.
  • Elevated homocysteine levels contribute to cardiovascular disease by damaging blood vessels, promoting oxidative stress, increasing blood clot formation, and contributing to atherosclerosis.

question_text: β-hydroxybutyric aciduria occurs due to:

Option D: Conversion of Propionyl CoA into Methyl malonyl CoA, done by Propionyl CoA Carboxylase, which require biotin as coenzyme (Biotin dependent Carboxylation Reaction)

  • Biotin functions to transfer carbon dioxide in a small number of reactions (carboxylation reaction).
  • A holocarboxylase synthetase catalyzes the transfer of biotin onto a lysine residue of the apoenzyme to form the biocytin residue of the holoenzyme.
  • The reactive intermediate is 1-N-carboxybiocytin, formed from bicarbonate in an ATP-dependent reaction.
  • The carboxyl group is then transferred to the substrate for carboxylation.
  • Biotin dependent Carboxylation (CO2 Fixation) Reactions: Requires biotin
    • Pyruvate Carboxylase: Pyruvate + CO2+ATP → Oxaloacetate +ADP +Pi
      • Important enzyme in gluconeogenic pathway
      • It also provides Oxaloacetate, which is catalyst for TCA cycle
    • Acetyl CoA Carboxylase: Acetyl CoA + CO2+ ATP→ Malonyl CoA + ADP + Pi
      • Acetyl CoA is starting material for synthesis of fatty acids
      • First step & Rate limiting reaction in fatty acid biosynthesis
    • Propionyl CoA Carboxylase: Propionyl CoA + CO2+ATP → Methyl malonyl CoA + ADP + Pi
      • Propionyl CoA is produced in metabolism of valine, isoleucine, threonine, methionine & degradation of odd chain fatty acids (Mnemonic - VOMIT).
      • Its further metabolism requires biotin.
    • β Methyl crotonyl CoA Carboxylase: β Methyl crotonyl CoA + CO2→ β Methyl glutaconyl CoA
      • Involved in metabolism of Leucine
    • It was once believed that all carboxylation reactions in biological system are dependent on biotin. This was later proved to be wrong. There are a few carboxylation reactions which do not require biotin termed as Biotin-Independent Carboxylation Reactions
    • Biotin Independent Carboxylation Reactions (do not require Biotin)
      • Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase, in urea cycle and pyrimidine synthesis
      • Addition of CO2 to form C6 in purine ring in de novo synthesis of purine nucleotide
      • Malic enzyme, converting pyruvate to malate.

question_text: A 40-year-old presented with edema around the metatarsal bone. Workup reveals hyperuricemia. Which is the major enzyme which plays a role in causing this?
explanation:
Explanation :

The presentation of acute inflammation and edema around the metatarsal bone (classic for podagra) with hyperuricemia is diagnostic of gout. The key enzyme directly responsible for the overproduction of uric acid in many cases is xanthine oxidase. This enzyme catalyzes the final two steps in the purine degradation pathway: the conversion of hypoxanthine to xanthine, and xanthine to uric acid. Overactivity of this enzyme, whether due to genetic factors, high cell turnover, or other reasons, leads directly to increased uric acid production.

Explanation of other options:

Thymidine kinase (Option B):This enzyme is involved in the salvage pathway of pyrimidine synthesis (specifically for thymidine) and has no role in purine metabolism or uric acid production.

PRPP synthetase (Option C): While overactivity of PRPP synthetase is a known but rare cause of purine overproduction and gout, it is not the "major" or most common enzymatic cause. Xanthine oxidase is the final common pathway for uric acid generation.

Alkaline phosphatase (Option D): This enzyme is a marker for bone and liver disease and is not involved in purine catabolism.

Key Takeaways:

  • Xanthine oxidase is the central enzyme catalyzing the production of uric acid from purines.
  • Gout results from the deposition of monosodium urate crystals in joints due to hyperuricemia.
  • Allopurinol, a xanthine oxidase inhibitor, is a primary treatment for gout.

question_text: The major process which produces purine nucleotide for synthesis of DNA during cell division is:
explanation:
Explanation:

The three processes that contribute to purine nucleotide biosynthesis are, in order of decreasing importance:

  1. Synthesis from amphibolic intermediates (De novo synthesis)
  2. Phosphoribosylation of purines (Salvage pathway)
  3. Phosphorylation of purine nucleosides (Salvage pathway)

De novo synthesis is the major pathway that provides nucleotides to tissues to meet the high physiological demands of DNA replication during cell division. In this pathway, purine nucleotides are built from scratch using precursors like amino acids (Glycine, Aspartate, Glutamine), CO2, and N10-Formyltetrahydrofolate.

Explanation of other options:

  • Dietary intake (Option A): Dietary nucleic acids and nucleotides are considered non-essential. They are generally not incorporated into tissue nucleic acids. Instead, they are degraded in the gut into purine bases, oxidized to uric acid, and excreted in the urine.
  • Phosphorylation of purines (Option C) & Phosphorylation of purine nucleosides (Option D): These processes describe the Salvage Pathway. This pathway recycles preformed purine bases (derived from the turnover of cellular nucleic acids) by adding ribose phosphate (via enzymes like HGPRT and APRT). While important for energy conservation and in tissues like the brain, it is secondary to de novo synthesis for bulk DNA production in dividing cells.

Key Takeaways:

  • De Novo Synthesis: Primary source of nucleotides for DNA synthesis; occurs mainly in the liver.
  • Salvage Pathway: Recycles bases; energetically less expensive. Defect causes Lesch-Nyhan Syndrome (HGPRT deficiency).
  • Dietary Purines: Converted to Uric Acid (waste), not reused.
  • Rate Limiting Enzyme (De Novo): Glutamine-PRPP Amidotransferase.

question_text: What condition is caused by a deficiency in the enzyme hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyl transferase (HGPRT)?
explanation:
Explanation:

HGPRT deficiency causes Lesch Nyhan syndrome, an X-linked recessive disorder in which failure of the purine salvage pathway leads to excess uric acid production and neurological symptoms like developmental delay and self-mutilation.

Gout involves hyperuricemia and is primarily linked to purine metabolism and the overproduction or underexcretion of uric acid. Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency is a urea cycle disorder leading to hyperammonemia and Adenosine deaminase deficiency is purine metabolism disorder but results in severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID).

question_text: Which of the following enzymes is deficient in the autosomal recessive type of severe combined immunodeficiency?
explanation:
Explanation:

Adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency is a cause of autosomal recessive Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID). ADA is an enzyme in the purine salvage pathway that deaminates adenosine and deoxyadenosine to inosine and deoxyinosine, respectively. Its deficiency leads to the accumulation of toxic metabolites, particularly deoxyadenosine triphosphate (dATP), which inhibits ribonucleotide reductase and arrests DNA synthesis. This is especially toxic to lymphocytes, leading to a profound deficiency of T-cells, B-cells, and NK cells (T-B-NK- SCID).

Explanation of other options:

Ornithine transcarbamylase (Option A): Its deficiency causes urea cycle disorder, not immunodeficiency.

Phosphomannose isomerase (Option B): Its deficiency causes carbohydrate-deficient glycoprotein syndrome.

Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyl transferase (HGPRT) (Option D): Its deficiency causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, characterized by hyperuricemia and neurological symptoms, not SCID.

Key Takeaways:

  • Adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency is a cause of autosomal recessive SCID.
  • It results in the accumulation of toxic purine metabolites that are lymphotoxic.

question_text: Allopurinol and Vitamin C are used to reduce uric acid production and prevent gout-like symptoms. Which of the following helps in the maturation of collagen?
explanation:
Explanation:

Ascorbic acid (Vitamin C) is essential for collagen maturation because it acts as a cofactor for the hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues.

  • This hydroxylation step is necessary for the stabilization of the collagen triple helix and for the formation of strong collagen fibers.
  • A deficiency of Vitamin C impairs this process, leading to scurvy, characterized by bleeding gums, poor wound healing, and fragile connective tissue.

Explanation of other options:

Proline (Option A): An important amino acid present in collagen that contributes to stability, but hydroxylation of proline (requiring Vitamin C) is the crucial step for proper maturation.

Copper and zinc (Option B): Trace elements needed for several enzymes, including lysyl oxidase (involved in collagen cross-linking), but they are not directly responsible for collagen maturation.

Phenylalanine (Option D): An amino acid precursor of tyrosine, involved in other metabolic pathways, but not directly linked to collagen maturation.

question_text: What is orotic aciduria primarily caused by?
option_b: Deficiency of OPRTase and OMP decarboxylase
explanation:
Explanation:

Orotic aciduria is caused by a deficiency of the enzymes orotate phosphoribosyltransferase (OPRTase) and orotidine-5'-monophosphate decarboxylase (OMP decarboxylase) in the de novo pyrimidine synthesis pathway.

Because of this defect, orotic acid cannot be converted into UMP, leading to its accumulation and excessive excretion in urine. Clinically, it presents with macrocytic megaloblastic anaemia, growth retardation and failure to thrive, without hyperammonemia (which helps differentiate it from urea cycle disorders).

question_text: Orotic aciduria occurs due to deficiency of all of the following enzyme except:
explanation:
Option A: Orotate phosphoribosyl transferase enzyme converts Orotic acid into OMP during pyrimidine biosynthesis. Type I orotic aciduria reflects a deficiency of both orotate phosphoribosyltransferase and orotidylate decarboxylase.

Option B: Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase enzyme converts dihydroorotic acid into Orotic acid. So involved in formation of orotic acid during pyrimidine biosynthesis.

Option C: Orotidylate decarboxylase enzyme converts OMP into UMP during pyrimidine biosynthesis. Type II orotic aciduria is due to a deficiency only of orotidylate decarboxylase.

Option D: Ornithine transcarbamylase is an enzyme involved in the urea cycle. Increased excretion of orotic acid, uracil, and uridine accompanies a deficiency in liver mitochondrial ornithine transcarbamoylase. Excess carbamoyl phosphate exits to the cytosol, where it stimulates pyrimidine nucleotide biosynthesis. The resulting mild orotic aciduria is increased by high-nitrogen foods.

Some other causes of Orotic aciduria are:

The orotic aciduria that accompanies the Reye syndrome probably is a consequence of the inability of severely damaged mitochondria to utilize carbamoyl phosphate, which then becomes available for cytosolic overproduction of orotic acid.

Some drugs May Precipitate Orotic Aciduria

Allopurinol, an alternative substrate for orotate phosphoribosyltransferase, competes with orotic acid. The resulting nucleotide product also inhibits orotidylate decarboxylase, resulting in orotic aciduria and proteinuria.

6-Azauridine, following conversion to 6-azauridine, also competitively inhibits orotidylate decarboxylase, enhancing excretion of orotic acid and orotidine.

question_text: A chronic alcoholic develops symptoms consistent with gouty arthritis. Which biochemical abnormality is most likely to be observed in this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

A chronic alcoholic who develops symptoms consistent with gouty arthritis will have increased urate and lactate levels.

Increased Uric Acid (Hyperuricemia):

  • Chronic alcohol consumption is a significant contributor to hyperuricemia, a condition characterised by elevated levels of uric acid in the blood. This occurs due to:
  • Increased turnover of purines from alcohol metabolism.
  • Decreased renal excretion of uric acid as lactate competes with uric acid for excretion through the kidneys.
  • These factors increase the likelihood of uric acid crystal deposition in joints, triggering gouty arthritis.

Increased Lactate Levels (Lactic Acidosis):

  • Alcohol metabolism, particularly through the enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase, generates an increased NADH/NAD+ ratio.
  • This shift favours the conversion of pyruvate to lactate, leading to lactic acidosis.
  • Elevated lactate levels further impair the kidneys' ability to excrete uric acid, exacerbating hyperuricemia and contributing to gout attacks.

Explanation for other options:

Decreased NADH/NAD+ ratio (Option A): Alcohol metabolism increases the NADH/NAD+ ratio, which indirectly contributes to lactate production and hyperuricemia.

Increased urea and urate levels (Option B): While urate levels increase, chronic alcohol use does not typically elevate urea levels unless there is concurrent kidney damage or protein metabolism disturbances.

Increased level of alkaline phosphatase (Option D): This is associated with conditions like bone or liver disease, but is not a key feature of gouty arthritis linked to alcohol consumption.

Reference:

  1. Is lactic acid a misunderstood trigger of gout attacks for a century? - ScienceDirect
  2. Gout Symptoms, Causes & Diet Recommendations | NIAMS

  2. Defect in pyrimidine nucleotide synthesis results in inhibition of DNA and RNA synthesis, which causes Megaloblastic anemia & Growth retardation

question_text: A tall, obese hypertensive patient was recently diagnosed with metabolic syndrome on routine workup. Which of the following is most likely to be found in this patient?
option_a: Increase in uric acid and insulin
option_c: Increase in triglycerides and total cholesterol
explanation:
Explanation:

Metabolic syndrome is primarily characterized by insulin resistance, which causes hyperglycemia and compensatory hyperinsulinemia. These metabolic disturbances are considered the central features of the syndrome, along with visceral obesity, hypertension, and dyslipidemia (high triglycerides, low HDL).

Learning Objective:

  • Metabolic syndrome is a cluster of risk factors that increase the risk for type 2 DM and ASCVD.
  • Diagnostic criteria (≥3 abnormalities):
    • Waist circumference >40 in (men) or >35 in (women)
    • Triglycerides ≥150 mg/dL
    • HDL <40 mg/dL (men) or <50 mg/dL (women)
    • Fasting glucose ≥100 mg/dL
    • BP ≥130/85 mmHg
  • Central mechanism: Visceral obesity → Insulin resistance → Hyperglycemia + Hyperinsulinemia.

Explanation of other options:

Increase in uric acid and insulin (Option A): Hyperuricemia can be associated, but it is not part of the diagnostic criteria. Insulin resistance is central, but uric acid elevation is not diagnostic.

Raised blood pressure and insulin (Option B): Hypertension is a component, but hyperglycemia/insulin resistance are the primary abnormalities.

Increase in triglycerides and total cholesterol (Option C): Metabolic syndrome typically involves high triglycerides and low HDL, not necessarily total cholesterol.

Key Takeaways:

  • Insulin resistance is the hallmark of metabolic syndrome.
  • Dyslipidemia typically = ↑ triglycerides + ↓ HDL (not ↑ total cholesterol).
  • Hyperuricemia may occur but is not diagnostic.
  • Management includes lifestyle changes, statins, antihypertensives, and insulin-sensitizing drugs (e.g., metformin, GLP-1 agonists).

References: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK459248/

question_text: Which enzyme is likely to be deficient in a 4-year-old child who presents with a habit of biting their lips and fingers, and has a missing portion of fingers on their left hand? Further evaluation shows delayed developmental milestones. The parents report that two male cousins on the mother's side have similar symptoms and have been diagnosed with a genetic disorder. Laboratory reports indicate hyperuricemia.
explanation:
Explanation:
The given clinical presentation is classic for Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, an X-linked recessive disorder caused by a deficiency of the enzyme hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyl transferase (HGPRT). This enzyme is vital for the purine salvage pathway. Its deficiency leads to:

  • Hyperuricemia:Due to increased de novo purine synthesis and breakdown.
  • Neurological symptoms:Severe intellectual disability, delayed milestones, self-mutilating behavior (biting lips and fingers), and aggressive tendencies.
  • X-linked inheritance:Explained by the history in male cousins on the maternal side.

The treatment for this condition include allopurinol for hyperuricemia and behaviour management using restraints for self-mutilation

Partial deficiency of HGPRT leads to Kelley-Seegmiller syndrome.

Explanation of other options:

Purine nucleoside phosphorylase (Option A): Its deficiency causes severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID), not self-mutilation or hyperuricemia.

Adenine phosphoribosyl transferase (Option C): Its deficiency causes 2,8-dihydroxyadenine urolithiasis (kidney stones), not neurological symptoms.

Adenosine deaminase (Option D): Its deficiency causes a form of severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID), also called Glanzmann-Riniker syndrome. They presents with severe bacterial,viral or fungal infections early in the life and presents with interstitial lung disease, chronic diarrhea and failure to thrive.

Key Takeaways:

  • Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is an X-linked disorder caused by HGPRT deficiency.
  • The triad includes hyperuricemia, severe neurological dysfunction, and self-mutilation.

question_text: A couple brings their 4-year-old child to the clinic due to concerns about self-injurious behavior and stunted growth. Which enzyme deficiency is most likely responsible for these symptoms?
explanation:
Explanation:

Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is a rare X-linked recessive disorder caused by a deficiency of the enzyme hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT). This enzyme plays a key role in the purine salvage pathway, and its absence results in excessive production of uric acid.

The condition is marked by self-injurious behavior, elevated uric acid levels (hyperuricemia), gout, neurological impairments, and impaired physical growth.

Explanation for other options:

Homogentisic Aciduria (Option B): Also known as alkaptonuria, this condition results from a deficiency of the enzyme homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase. It leads to dark-colored urine, ochronosis (dark pigmentation in connective tissues), and early-onset arthritis. However, it is not associated with self-injurious behavior or growth delays.

Phenylalanine Hydroxylase Deficiency (Option C): This enzyme deficiency leads to phenylketonuria (PKU), characterized by intellectual disability, seizures, and light skin and hair due to hypopigmentation. It does not involve hyperuricemia or self-mutilation.

Adenosine Deaminase Deficiency (Option D): Caused by mutations in the ADA gene, this rare disorder leads to a severe combined immunodeficiency due to a lack of functional B and T lymphocytes. Symptoms typically appear before six months of age and include frequent infections, failure to thrive, chronic diarrhea, and skin rashes. It is not associated with behavioral issues like self-mutilation.

question_text: RNAs are far less stable than DNA due to presence of:
explanation:
DNA & RNA are polynucleotides 

The 5′-phosphoryl group of a mononucleotide can esterify a second hydroxyl group, forming a phosphodiester. Most commonly, this second hydroxyl group is the 3′-OH of the pentose of a second nucleotide. This forms a dinucleotide in which the pentose moieties are linked by a 3′,5′-phosphodiester bond to form the “backbone” of RNA and DNA. 

Hydrolysis of the phosphodiester bond is strongly favoured on thermodynamic grounds, but still in the absence of catalysis by phosphodiesterase, hydrolysis of the phosphodiester bonds of DNA occurs only over long periods of time. DNA therefore persists for considerable periods, and has been detected even in fossils. 

RNAs are far less stable than DNA since the 2′-hydroxyl group of RNA (absent from DNA) functions as a nucleophile during hydrolysis of the 3′,5′-phosphodiester bond.

Option C: RNA is single stranded and DNA is double stranded, but number of strands will not affect stability of nucleic acid

Option D: RNA contain sugar ribose and DNA contains sugar Deoxyribose.

question_text: The two strands of double-stranded helix are held together by all of the following interaction, except
explanation:

question_text: What is the term for a single mutation in a nucleotide base pair that leads to formation of termination codon?
explanation:
Explanation:

A nonsense mutation is a point mutation in which a codon specifying an amino acid is changed to a stop codon, leading to premature termination of translation and typically producing a truncated, nonfunctional protein.

Explanation of Incorrect Options:

  • Missense mutation (Option A):In a missense mutation, a single nucleotide change substitutes one amino acid for another, altering the protein's structure but not terminating translation prematurely.
  • Stop mutation (Option C):While this term is occasionally used informally as a synonym for nonsense mutation, it is not the standard term in genetics. The preferred term is "nonsense mutation".
  • Silent mutation (Option D):Silent (synonymous) mutations alter the DNA sequence without changing the amino acid due to the redundancy of the genetic code. Translation continues as normal

question_text: Primosome is a mobile complex between:
explanation:
Several Okazaki fragments (up to 1000) must be sequentially synthesized for each replication fork. As the synthesis of an Okazaki fragment is completed and the polymerase is released, a new primer has been synthesized. The same polymerase molecule remains associated with the replication fork and proceeds to synthesize the next Okazaki fragment.

Human BRCA1 and BRCA2 are large proteins that interact with a wide range of other proteins involved in transcription, chromosome maintenance, DNA repair, and control of the cell cycle. BRCA2 has been implicated in the recombinational DNA repair of double-strand breaks. However, the precise molecular function of BRCA1 and BRCA2 in these various cellular processes is not yet clear. Bloom Syndrome

Bloom syndrome results from a mutation in the BLM gene, which encodes a RecQ helicase vital for repairing DNA double-strand breaks.

Clinical Features:

  • Physical: Short stature, narrow facial structure, small jaw, large ears, and a high-pitched voice.
  • Skin: Red rash appears on sun-exposed areas such as the face, arms, and hands, along with dilated blood vessels and patches of both lighter and darker skin.
  • Development: Patients often experience learning difficulties, fertility issues, and delays in growth and development.
  • Infections: There is a tendency toward frequent ear and lung infections.
  • Other Conditions: Increased risk of diabetes and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).

Cancer Risk:

Individuals with Bloom syndrome have a higher likelihood of developing early-onset cancers, including squamous cell carcinoma of the skin, leukemia, lymphoma, and gastrointestinal cancers.

Xeroderma Pigmentosum (Option B): An autosomal recessive disorder characterized by extreme sensitivity to sunlight, with about 50% of patients experiencing severe burning even after minimal sun exposure. UV radiation causes cross-linking of pyrimidine bases, which disrupts normal DNA replication. Nucleotide excision repair (NER) is responsible for correcting this damage, and inherited loss-of-function mutations in any NER genes lead to xeroderma pigmentosum. Most patients develop freckling (lentigines) on sun-exposed areas before the age of two. There is a markedly increased risk of sunlight-induced skin cancers-such as basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and melanoma- at a young age.

Cockayne Syndrome (Option C): This condition involves defects in transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair, causing photosensitivity, growth retardation, and neurodevelopmental problems. However, it does not affect double-strand break repair.

Lynch Syndrome (Option D): Also known as hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC), Lynch syndrome is caused by mutations in mismatch repair genes (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2). It is not associated with childhood growth delays or learning difficulties.

question_text: A number of different DNA polymerase molecules engage in DNA replication. All of them share following properties, except:
explanation:
A number of different DNA polymerase molecules engage in DNA replication. These share three important properties: (1) chain elongation (Option A), (2) processivity (Option B), and (3) proofreading (Option C).

Chain elongation accounts for the rate (in nucleotides per second; nt/s) at which polymerization occurs. Processivity is an expression of the number of nucleotides added to the nascent chain before the polymerase disengages from the template.

The proofreading function identifies copying errors and corrects them.

Option D: DNA ligase is involved in sealing of the single-strand nick between the nascent chain and Okazaki fragments on lagging strands at termination of replication.

In E. coli, DNA polymerase III (pol III) functions at the replication fork. Of all polymerases, it catalyzes the highest rate of chain elongation and is the most processive. It is capable of polymerizing 0.5 Mb of DNA during one cycle on the leading strand. Pol III is a large (>1 MDa), multisubunit protein complex in E. coli. DNA pol III associates with the two identical β subunits of the DNA sliding 'clamp'; this association dramatically increases pol III-DNA complex stability, processivity (100 to >50,000 nucleotides) and rate of chain elongation (20-50 nt/s) generating the high degree of processivity the enzyme exhibits.

Polymerase I (pol I) and II (pol II) are mostly involved in proofreading and DNA repair. Eukaryotic cells have counterparts for each of these enzymes plus a large number of additional DNA polymerases primarily involved in DNA repair.

In mammalian cells, the polymerase is capable of polymerizing at a rate that is somewhat slower than the rate of polymerization of deoxynucleotides by the bacterial DNA polymerase complex. This reduced rate may result from interference by nucleosomes.

Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32nd edition CH 35 PN 364

question_text: DNA replication occurs during which phase of cell cycle?
explanation:
Option A: Cell prepares for DNA synthesis in G1.

Option B: Cell prepares for mitosis in G2.

Option C: During S phase, replication of the DNA genome takes place, so referred as Synthetic phase.

Option D: During M phase, mitosis occurs, so referred as Mitotic phase

In eukaryotic cells, including human cells, the replication of the DNA genome occurs only at a specified time during the life span of the cell. This period is referred to as the synthetic or S phase. This is usually temporally separated from the mitotic, or M phase, by nonsynthetic periods referred to as gap 1 (G1) and gap 2 (G2) phases, occurring before and after the S phase, respectively. Among other things, the cell prepares for DNA synthesis in G1, and for mitosis in G2. The cell regulates DNA synthesis by allowing it to occur only once per cell cycle, and only during S phase, in cells preparing to divide by a mitotic process.

Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32nd edition CH 35 PN 368

question_text:

Option D: DHU Arm (D arm): named due to presence of a dihydrouridine (DHU) in this area. It is a recognition site for the enzyme which adds amino acid to t RNA.

Transfer RNA

  • About 15% of the total RNA in the cell.
  • They are easily soluble, also k/a soluble RNA or sRNA. 
  • They are present in the cytoplasm
  • General structure is similar to other RNA. Additionally have some typical structural characteristics.

Typical Structural Characteristics:

  • Smallest of the three major type of RNA molecule (73-93 nucleotides in length)
  • Contain some unusual bases (eg Dihydrouracil, Pseudouridine & hypoxanthine).
  • Have extensive internal base-pairing that produces characteristic structure (Clover leaf like structure)
  • In their structure, they have 5 different parts (5 arms), which differ in structure & function.
  1. Acceptor Arm: It carries the amino acid. At the 3' End, it has 7 base pairs. The end sequence is CCA-3'. Each tRNA serves as an “adaptor” molecule that carries its specific amino acid—covalently attached to its 3'-end—to the site of protein synthesis
  2. Anticodon Arm: Present at opposite side of the acceptor arm. It recognizes the codon present in mRNA. It has base sequences complementary to mRNA codon. The specificity of tRNA is in anticodon sites.
  3. DHU Arm (D arm): named due to presence of a dihydrouridine (DHU) in this area. It is a recognition site for the enzyme which adds amino acid to t RNA.
  4. Pseudouridine Arm: Opposite to DHU arm, named as it contains pseudouridine. It involved in binding tRNA to ribosomes
  5. About 75% of tRNA molecules possess a short extra arm.

Function:

  • Transfer amino acids from cytoplasm to ribosome for protein synthesis; so k/a transfer RNA
  • It recognizes the genetic code on mRNA, which specifies specific amino acids.
  • At least 20 species of tRNA molecules in every cell, at least one (and often several) corresponding to each of the 20 amino acids required for protein synthesis

question_text: All of the following attachment proteins indirectly interact fibronectin receptor with actin microfilaments, except:
explanation:
• Fibronectin is a major glycoprotein of the extracellular matrix, also found in a soluble form in plasma. It consists of two identical subunits, each of about 230 kDa, joined by two disulfide bridges near their carboxyl terminals.
  • The gene encoding fibronectin is very large, containing some 50 exons; the RNA produced by its transcription is subject to considerable alternative splicing, and as many as 20 different mRNAs have been detected in various tissues.
  • Fibronectin contains three types of repeating motifs (I, II, and III), which are organized into functional domains (at least seven); functions of these domains include binding fibronectin (enabling molecules of the protein to interact) heparin, fibrin, collagen, and cell surfaces.
  • Fibronectin binds to cells via a transmembrane receptor protein which belongs to the integrin class of proteins. Fibronectin contains an Arg-Gly-Asp (RGD) sequence that binds to the integrin receptor. This sequence is shared by a number of other proteins present in the ECM that bind to integrins present in cell plasma membranes, and its presence in synthetic peptides enables them to inhibit the binding of fibronectin to cells.

Option A, Option B & Option C: The fibronectin receptor interacts indirectly with actin microfilaments present in the cytosol via a number of proteins, collectively known as attachment proteins; these include talin, vinculin, α-actinin, and paxillin. Such large protein complexes form focal adhesions which not only anchor cells in the ECM, but also relay signals from the exterior which influence cell behaviour. Thus, the interaction of fibronectin with its receptor provides one route whereby the outside of the cell can communicate with the inside.

Fibronectin is also involved in cell migration, as it provides a binding site for cells and thus helps them to steer their way through the ECM. The amount of fibronectin around many transformed cells is sharply reduced, partly explaining their faulty interaction with the ECM.

Option D: Elastin is a connective tissue protein that is responsible for properties of extensibility and elastic recoil in tissues. Although not as widespread as collagen, elastin is present in large amounts in tissues that require these physical properties, for example, lung, large arterial blood vessels, and some elastic ligaments. Smaller quantities of elastin are also found in skin, ear cartilage, and several other tissues.

question_text: RNA synthesis is different from DNA synthesis in following ways, except:
option_a: No efficient proofreading function during RNA synthesis
option_b: Primer is not involved in RNA synthesis
option_c: DNA synthesis occurs with 5-3 polarity, whereas RNA synthesis occurs with 3-5 polarity
option_d: U replaces T as the complementary base for A in RNA synthesis
explanation:
The statement "Primer is not involved in RNA synthesis" (Option B) is the exception because RNA synthesis does indeed involve a primer, just like DNA synthesis.

Here's the justification for each option:

A) No efficient proofreading function during RNA synthesis:

  • Justification: This statement is correct. RNA polymerases do not have an efficient proofreading function like DNA polymerases. This lack of proofreading contributes to the higher error rate in RNA synthesis.

B) Primer is not involved in RNA synthesis:

  • Justification: This statement is incorrect. RNA synthesis, like DNA synthesis, also involves the use of a primer. In both cases, a short RNA primer is needed to initiate synthesis by RNA polymerase or DNA polymerase.

C) DNA synthesis occurs with 5-3 polarity, whereas RNA synthesis occurs with 3-5 polarity:

  • Justification: This statement is correct. DNA synthesis occurs in the 5' to 3' direction, while RNA synthesis occurs in the 3' to 5' direction. This difference is due to the antiparallel nature of DNA and RNA strands.

D) U replaces T as the complementary base for A in RNA synthesis:

  • Justification: This statement is correct. In RNA synthesis, uracil (U) replaces thymine (T) as the complementary base for adenine (A). RNA uses A-U base pairs, while DNA uses A-T base pairs.

In summary, Option B is the exception because a primer is indeed involved in RNA synthesis, similar to DNA synthesis.

Reference: Harper’s illustrated biochemistry 32nd edition CH 36 PN 375

question_text: All of the following are post transcriptional modification done for messenger RNA, except:
option_d: Attachment of CCA terminal at the 3' end

Messenger RNA Is Modified at the 5’ & 3’ Ends

Option A: The Coding Portions (Exons) of Most Eukaryotic mRNA Encoding Genes Are Interrupted by Introns, so Introns Are Removed & Exons Are Spliced Together during formation of mRNA molecules.

Option B: Eukaryotic mRNAs contain a 7-methylguanosine cap structure at their 5′ terminus. The cap structure is added to the 5′ end of the newly transcribed mRNA precursor in the nucleus very soon after synthesis and prior to transport of the mRNA molecule to the cytoplasm. The 5′ cap of the RNA transcript is required both for efficient translation initiation and protection of the 5′ end of mRNA from attack by 5′ → 3′ exonucleases. The secondary methylations of mRNA molecules, those on the 2′-hydroxy and the N7 of adenylyl residues, occur after the mRNA molecule has appeared in the cytoplasm. 

Option C: Eukaryotic mRNAs also have a poly(A) tail at the 3′ terminus. Poly(A) tails are added to the 3′ end of mRNA molecules in a posttranscriptional processing step. Following nuclear transport, cytoplasmic enzymes in mammalian cells can both add and remove adenylyl residues from the poly(A) tails; this process has been associated with an alteration of mRNA stability and translatability.

Option D: Attachment of the CCA terminal at the 3′ end is done in tRNA, not in mRNA. The characteristic CpCpAOH terminal at the 3′ end of the tRNA is attached by the enzyme nucleotidyl transferase. The 3′ OH of the A ribose is the point of attachment for the specific amino acid that is to enter the polymerization reaction of protein synthesis. The methylation of mammalian tRNA precursors probably occurs in the nucleus, whereas the cleavage and attachment of CpCpAOH are cytoplasmic functions, since the terminal nucleotides turn over more rapidly than do the tRNA molecules themselves. Specific aminoacyl tRNA synthetases within the cytoplasm of mammalian cells are required for the attachment of the different amino acids to the CpCpAOH residues.

The tRNA molecules serve as adapters for the translation of the information in the sequence of nucleotides of the mRNA into specific amino acids. There are at least 20 species of tRNA molecules in every cell, at least one (and often several) corresponding to each of the 20 amino acids required for protein synthesis.

Although each specific tRNA differs from the others in its sequence of nucleotides, the tRNA molecules as a class have many features in common. The primary structure-that is, the nucleotide sequence-of all tRNA molecules allows extensive folding and intrastrand complementarity to generate a secondary structure that appears in two dimensions like a cloverleaf. 

All tRNA molecules contain four main double-stranded arms or stems, connected by single-stranded loops named for their respective nucleotide composition or function. The acceptor arm terminates in the nucleotides CpCpAOH. These three nucleotides are added post transcriptionally by a specific nucleotidyl transferase enzyme. The tRNA-appropriate amino acid is attached, or “charged,” onto the 3′-OH group of the A moiety of the acceptor arm through the action of specific aminoacyl tRANA synthetases. The D, TψC, and extra arms help define a specific tRNA. tRNAs comprise roughly 20% of total cellular RNA.

question_text: Degeneracy of genetic code means:
option_a: Multiple codons decode the same amino acid
option_b: Single codon decode for two amino acid
option_c: First nucleotide in codon responsible for degeneracy of codon
option_d: For a specific codon, only a single amino acid is indicated
explanation:
Option A: Degeneracy in the genetic code is when multiple codons decode the same amino acid.

Some amino acids are encoded by several codons; for example, six different codons, UCU, UCC, UCA, UCG, AGU, and AGC all specify serine. Other amino acids, such as methionine and tryptophan, have a single codon.

Option B: For any specific codon, only a single amino acid is specified. Single codon never decodes for two amino acids during protein synthesis.

Option C: In general, the third nucleotide in a codon is less important than the first two in determining the specific amino acid to be incorporated, and this accounts for most of the degeneracy of the code.

Option D: For any specific codon, only a single amino acid is specified; with rare exceptions, the genetic code is unambiguous-that is, given a specific codon, only a single amino acid is indicated. However, it does not explain degeneracy.

The genetic code is virtually universal. An exception occurs in mitochondria, in which a few codons have meanings different than those shown in table.

question_text: Spliceosomes consists of all of the following small nuclear RNA except,
explanation:
A special multicomponent complex, the spliceosome, is involved in converting the primary transcript into mRNA. Spliceosomes consist of the primary transcript, five snRNAs (U1, U2, U4, U5, and U6), and more than 60 proteins, many of which contain conserved RRM (RNA recognition) and SR (serine–arginine) protein motifs. Collectively, the five snRNAs and RRM/SR-containing proteins form a small nuclear ribonucleoprotein termed an snRNP complex.

The snRNAs and associated proteins are required for formation of the various structures and intermediates. U1 within the snRNP complex binds first by base pairing to the 5′ exon–intron boundary. U2 within the snRNP complex then binds by base pairing to the branch site, and this exposes the nucleophilic A residue. U4/U5/U6 within the snRNP complex mediates an ATP-dependent protein-mediated unwinding that results in disruption of the base-paired U4–U6 complex with the release of U4. U6 is then able to interact first with U2, then with U1. These interactions serve to approximate the 5′–splice site, the branch point with its reactive A, and the 3′–splice site. This alignment is enhanced by U5. This process also results in the formation of the loop or lariat structure. The two ends are cleaved, probably by the U2–U6 within the snRNP complex. U6 is certainly essential, since yeast cells deficient in this snRNA are not viable. It is important to note that RNA serves as the catalytic agent. This sequence of events is then repeated in genes containing multiple introns. In such cases, a definite pattern is followed for each gene, though the introns are not necessarily removed in sequence—1, then 2, then 3, etc.

So five snRNAs (U1, U2, U4, U5, and U6) are present in spliceosomes, U3 is not present.

So option C is correct, others are incorrect.

Reference: Harper’s illustrated biochemistry 32nd edition CH 36 PN 388

question_text: Which of the following enzymes lead to synthesis of DNA from RNA?

Option A: DNA Polymerase leads to synthesizing DNA from DNA (Replication of DNA).

Option B: RNA polymerase leads to synthesis of RNA from DNA (transcription).

Option C: Peptidyl transferase is an enzyme that leads to synthesis of protein (translation).

Option D: reverse transcriptase is RNA-dependent DNA polymerase, a class of enzymes capable of synthesizing a single-stranded and then a dsDNA molecule from a single-stranded RNA template. It exists in retroviruses.

The genetic material for some animal and plant viruses is RNA rather than DNA. Although some RNA viruses never have their information transcribed into a DNA molecule, many animal RNA viruses—specifically, the retroviruses (eg, the human immunodeficiency, or HIV virus)—are transcribed by viral RNA–dependent DNA polymerase, the so-called reverse transcriptase, to produce a double-stranded DNA copy of their RNA genome. In many cases, the resulting double-stranded DNA transcript is integrated into the host genome and subsequently serves as a template for gene expression and from which new viral RNA genomes and viral mRNAs can be transcribed.

question_text: A 13-year-old child presents with acute flaccid paralysis. To confirm a diagnosis of poliomyelitis, a Reverse Transcriptase-PCR (RT-PCR) is performed on a CSF sample. Which of the following enzymes is essential for the initial step of this diagnostic test?
explanation:
Explanation:
The correct enzyme is RNA-dependent DNA polymerase (Reverse Transcriptase). The first step of RT-PCR is Reverse Transcription, where the viral RNA genome is used as a template to synthesize a complementary DNA (cDNA) strand. This critical step is performed by the enzyme RNA-dependent DNA polymerase (Reverse Transcriptase). Only after this step can the standard PCR (which uses a DNA-dependent DNA polymerase) amplify the DNA.

Explanation of other options:

DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (Option A): This enzyme (e.g., RNA Pol II) transcribes DNA into RNA and is not used in RT-PCR.

DNA-dependent DNA polymerase (Option C): This enzyme (e.g., Taq polymerase) is used in the second step of RT-PCR to amplify the cDNA, but it is not the enzyme that performs the initial reverse transcription.

RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (Option D): This enzyme is used by RNA viruses (like the poliovirus itself) to replicate their RNA genome inside the host cell, but it is not used in the RT-PCR laboratory technique.

Key Takeaways:

  • RT-PCR Step 1: RNA → cDNA (uses Reverse Transcriptase/RNA-dependent DNA polymerase).
  • RT-PCR Step 2: Amplify cDNA (uses DNA-dependent DNA polymerase).

question_text: DNA methylation is not related to?
explanation:
DNA methylation is a process in which a methyl group is added to the cytosine base in DNA. This process can affect gene expression, but it is not directly related to capping.

Capping is a process in which a guanine nucleotide is added to the 5' end of an mRNA molecule. This process helps to protect the mRNA molecule from degradation and helps to ensure that it is translated correctly.

The other options are all related to DNA methylation:

  • Mismatch repair is a process that corrects errors in DNA replication. DNA methylation can affect mismatch repair by preventing the repair machinery from accessing methylated DNA.
  • DNA replication is the process of making a copy of DNA. DNA methylation can affect DNA replication by affecting the binding of DNA replication proteins to DNA.
  • Gene silencing is the process of turning off gene expression. DNA methylation can silence genes by preventing the binding of transcription factors to DNA.

question_text: Which of the following is not a characteristic of enhancer during regulation of β-interferon gene?

explanation:
Option A: Certain DNA elements facilitate or enhance initiation at the promoter and hence are termed enhancers. Enhancer elements, which typically contain multiple binding sites for transactivator proteins, differ from the promoter in notable ways.

Option B: Work when located long distances from the promoter. They can exert their positive influence on transcription even when separated by tens of thousands of base pairs from a promoter;

Option C: Work when oriented in either direction, work upstream (5′) or downstream (3′) from the promoter.

Other features of enhancers are:

Work by binding one or more proteins

Work by recruiting chromatin-modifying coregulatory complexes

Work by facilitating binding or function of the basal transcription complex at the cis-linked promoter

One of the best-understood mammalian enhancer systems is that of the β-interferon gene. This gene is induced on viral infection of mammalian cells. One goal of the cell, once virally infected, is to attempt to mount an antiviral response to save the infected cell, then to help to save the entire organism from viral infection.

question_text: Frameshift mutation can occur due to all of the following except:
option_a: Insertion of one nucleotide in DNA
option_b: Insertion of two nucleotides in DNA
option_c: Deletion of one nucleotide in DNA
explanation:
Option A & Option B:

Insertions of one or two (or non-multiples of three nucleotides) into a gene result in an mRNA in which the reading frame is distorted upon translation, and the same effects that occur with deletions are reflected in the mRNA translation. This may result in garbled amino acid sequences distal to the insertion and the generation of a nonsense codon at, or distal to the insertion, or perhaps reading through the normal termination codon.

Option C: The deletion of a single nucleotide from the coding strand of a gene results in an altered reading frame in the mRNA. The machinery translating the mRNA does not recognize that a base was missing, since there is no punctuation in the reading of codons. Thus, a major alteration in the sequence of polymerized amino acids results. Altering the reading frame results in a garbled translation of the mRNA distal to the single nucleotide deletion. Not only is the sequence of amino acids distal to this deletion garbled, but reading of the message can also result in the appearance of a nonsense codon and thus the production of a polypeptide both garbled and prematurely terminated.

Option D: Single-base substitution (point mutations) can lead to silent, missense or nonsense mutation.

A hematoma is a localised collection of blood outside of blood vessels, usually due to trauma or injury. It is not related to iron toxicity or iron overload.

Causes of Iron Overload

  • Hereditary Hemochromatosis:
    • A genetic condition where mutations (commonly in the HFE gene) lead to increased iron absorption from the diet, even when iron levels are adequate.
    • This is one of the most common causes of iron overload, especially in populations of European descent.

question_text: Differential expression of B-48 in the intestinal epithelial cells is due to?
explanation:
Option A: Coding information can be changed at the mRNA level by RNA editing. In such cases, the coding sequence of the mRNA differs from that in the cognate DNA.

An example is the apolipoprotein B(apoB) gene and mRNA. In the liver, the single apoB gene is transcribed into an mRNA that directs the synthesis of a 100-kDa protein, apoB100. In the intestine, the same gene directs the synthesis of the identical mRNA primary transcript; however, a cytidine deaminase converts a CAA codon in the mRNA to UAA at a single specific site. Rather than encoding glutamine, this codon becomes a termination signal and hence production of a truncated 48-kDa protein(apoB48) results. ApoB100 and apoB48 have different functions in the two organs.

A growing number of other examples include a glutamine to arginine change in the glutamate receptor and several changes in trypanosome mitochondrial mRNAs, generally involving the addition or deletion of uridine.

The exact extent of RNA editing genome wide is unknown, but current estimates suggest that perhaps 0.01% of mRNAs are edited in this fashion. Recently, editing of miRNAs has been described suggesting that these two forms of post-transcriptional control mechanisms could cooperatively contribute to gene regulation.

Option B: RNA interference(RNAi) or Post-Transcriptional Gene Silencing(PTGS) is a conserved biological response to double-stranded RNA that mediates resistance to both endogenous parasitic and exogenous pathogenic nucleic acids and regulates the expression of protein-coding genes.

Option C: Tissue-specific regulation of gene expression can be provided by alternative splicing. The glucokinase(GK) gene consists of 10 exons interrupted by 9 introns.

Moreover, as noted above, such variation in spliced mRNAs can also change the protein coding protein potential of these mRNAs.

Option D: DNA processing is not involved in differential expression of B-48 in the intestinal epithelial cells.

question_text: RNAi acts through?
explanation:
Targeted Gene Regulation by Disruption or Knockout, Knockin, Editing, and Controlled Expression

Various technical advances have allowed for the precise, targeted modification of mammalian genes. The exact methods used for genetically engineering mammalian genomes have evolved from tedious, low-efficiency methods based on positive and negative drug selections and homologous recombination (Knockout/Knockin) to the recently described CRISPR-Cas9 system. The goal of all of these methods is ultimately to generate a family of genetic variants of a gene of interest that are (a) a null, or complete loss-of-function allele; (b) recessive, loss-of-function alleles; and (c) ideally, dominant gain-of-function alleles. These genetic alterations are generated in pluripotent stem cells, which ultimately allow for introduction and propagation in whole model organisms (flys, fish, worms, rodents, etc). Having all three of these genetic variants allows one to precisely dissect the mechanism of action of any gene. However, complicating genetic analyses of many genes is the fact that their function(s) are essential for viability. To get around this problem, cell-type or tissue-specific genetic variants must be generated. This hurdle has been overcome through the use of cell- and tissue-specific enhancers that can drive the conditional (ie, experimentally controlled) expression of the targeting recombinases (ie, CRE-lox) and/or or nuclease (CRISPR-Cas9) that generate the altered genes, either null or loss- or gain-of-function alleles.

Alternatively, selected loss-of-function alleles can be generated through equivalent siRNA expression to knock down production of a specific gene product. Collectively, these methods allow for sophisticated genetic and biochemical tests of gene function and allow scientists to probe the structure and function of mammalian genes in physiologic contexts. Tremendous molecular mechanistic insights have been, and will continue to be, obtained into the molecular etiology of human disease through these and other biochemical approaches.

So option B is correct.

question_text: Operon, the unit of genetic expression consists of:
explanation:
Jacob and Monod in 1961 described their operon model in a classic paper. Their hypothesis was to a large extent based on observations on the regulation of lactose metabolism by the intestinal bacterium E. coli. The molecular mechanisms responsible for the regulation of the genes involved in the metabolism of lactose are now among the best-understood in any organism.

β-Galactosidase hydrolyzes the β-galactoside lactose to galactose and glucose. The gene encoding β-galactosidase (lacZ) is clustered with the genes encoding lactose permease (lacY) and thiogalactoside transacetylase (lacA).

The genes encoding these three enzymes, along with the lac promoter and lac operator (a regulatory region), and the lacI gene encoding the LacI repressor are physically linked and constitute the lac operon.

So the operon model consists of related genes (Option A) along with operator (Option B) and promoter (Option C) sequences.

question_text: Overlay blot technique is used to detect:
option_c: Size and quantify specific RNA molecules
option_d: Size and quantify specific protein molecules

Option A: 

Overlay blot examines protein–protein interactions.

In this technique, proteins are separated by electrophoresis, blotted to a membrane, renatured, and analysed for an interaction with a protein by incubation with a specific labelled protein probe (overlay assay) using either a labelled protein, or alternatively protein–protein interactions are detected using a specific antibody.

Option B: 

Southwestern examines protein–nucleic acid interactions. 

In this technique, proteins are separated by electrophoresis, blotted to a membrane, renatured, and analysed for an interaction with a particular DNA or RNA sequence. 

Option C: 

Northern blot transfer technique is used to size and quantify specific RNA molecules.

Option D:

Western blot transfer technique is used to size and quantify specific protein molecules.

Blotting & Probing Techniques Allow Visualization of Specific Target Molecules

Visualization of a specific DNA or RNA fragment or protein among the many thousands of contaminating non-target molecules in a complex sample requires the convergence of a number of techniques, collectively termed blot transfer.

The first technique is named for the person who devised the technique, Edward Southern; the other names began as laboratory jargon, but are now accepted terms. These procedures are useful in determining how many copies of a gene are in a given tissue or whether there are any alterations in a gene (deletions, insertions, or rearrangements) because the requisite, initial gel electrophoresis step separates the molecules on the basis of size. Occasionally, if a specific base is changed and a restriction site is altered, these procedures can detect a point mutation. The Northern and Western blot transfer techniques are used to size and quantify specific RNA and protein molecules, respectively.

A fourth technique, the Southwestern or overlay blot, which examines protein–nucleic acid interactions or protein–protein interactions, respectively are variants of the Southern/Northern/ Western blotting methods.

Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32nd edition CH 39 PN 438

question_text: In addition to Taq polymerases, PCR requires all of the following, except:
explanation:
Option A: Template DNA is used as a target DNA to amplify specific sequences.

Option B: All four Deoxyribonucleotide triphosphate is used in PCR, which are polymerized by DNA polymerase.

Option C: Primers that hybridize to complementary sequences on opposite strands of DNA and flank the target sequence.

Option D: Primase is not used in PCR.

The Polymerase Chain Reaction Method Amplifies DNA Sequences 

PCR is a method of amplifying a target sequence of DNA. The development of PCR has revolutionized the ways in which both DNA and RNA can be studied. PCR provides a sensitive, selective, and extremely rapid means of amplifying any desired sequence of DNA. Specificity is based on the use of two oligonucleotide primers that hybridize to complementary sequences on opposite strands of DNA and flank the target sequence. 

The DNA sample is first heat denatured (>90°C) to separate the two strands of the template DNA containing the target sequence; the primers, added in excess, are allowed to anneal to the DNA (typically at 50-75°C) in order to generate the required template-primer complex. Subsequently, each strand is copied by a DNA polymerase, starting at the primer sites in the presence of all four dXTPs. The two DNA strands each serve as a template for the synthesis of new DNA from the two primers. Repeated cycles of heat denaturation, annealing of the primers to their complementary sequences, and extension of the annealed primers with DNA polymerase result in the exponential amplification of DNA segments of defined length. Product DNA doubles with each PCR cycle. DNA synthesis is catalyzed by a heat-stable DNA polymerase purified from one of a number of different thermophilic bacteria, organisms that grow at 70 to 80°C. Thermostable DNA polymerases withstand short incubations at over 90°, temperatures required to completely denature DNA. These thermostable DNA polymerases have made automation of PCR possible.

DNA sequences as short as 50 to 100 bp and as long as 10 kb can readily be amplified by PCR. Twenty cycles provide an amplification of 106 (ie, 220) and 30 cycles, 109 (230). Each cycle takes ≤5 to 10 minutes so that even large DNA molecules can be amplified fairly rapidly. Because of subtle differences in DNA sequence with each new PCR target, the exact conditions for amplification must be empirically optimized. 

Application of PCR:

The workhorse PCR technique is central to many DNA/RNA sequencing technologies. 

The PCR method allows the DNA in a single cell, hair follicle, or spermatozoon to be amplified and analyzed. Thus, the applications of PCR to forensic medicine are obvious. 

PCR is also used, 

  1. To detect and quantify infectious agents, especially latent viruses; 
  2. To make prenatal genetic diagnoses; 
  3. To detect allelic polymorphisms ranging from single base pair changes to large and small indels and gene amplification; 
  4. To establish precise tissue types for transplants; and 
  5. To study evolution, using DNA from archeological samples 
  6. For quantitative RNA analyses after RNA copying and mRNA quantitation by the so-called RT-PCR method (cDNA copies of mRNA generated by a retroviral reverse transcriptase)
  7. To score in vivo protein-DNA occupancy using chromatin immunoprecipitation assays. New uses of PCR are developed every year.

Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32nd edition CH 39 PN 440

question_text: If a polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplification is run for 26 cycles, how many cycles would yield exactly half the number of DNA copies produced at 26 cycles?
explanation:
Explanation:

At 25 cycles the yield will be exactly half of that after 26th as PCR amplification is exponential, following the formula:

Number of copies = 2n, where n is the number of cycles.

  • Copies after 26 cycles = 226
  • Half of this amount = 226 / 2 = 226 x 2-1 = 225
  • Therefore, the number of cycles needed to get half the copies is 25 cycles.

Key Takeaways:

  • Each PCR cycle doubles the number of DNA molecules. Therefore, one cycle less gives half the amount.

question_text: Which of the following can lead to Denaturation of DNA?
explanation:
The double-stranded structure of DNA can be separated into two component strands in solution by increasing the temperature or decreasing the salt concentration. Not only do the two stacks of bases pull apart, but the bases themselves unstack while still connected in the polymer by the phosphodiester backbone.

Option A: DNA can be denatured by increasing temperature

The strands of a given molecule of DNA separate over a temperature range. The midpoint is called the melting temperature, or Tm. The Tm is influenced by the base composition of the DNA and by the salt concentration of the solution. DNA rich in G–C pairs, which has three hydrogen bonds, melts at a higher temperature than DNA rich in A–T pairs, which has two hydrogen bonds. A 10-fold increase of monovalent cation concentration increases the Tm by 16.6°C by neutralizing the intrinsic inter chain repulsion between the highly negatively charged.

Option B: DNA can be denatured by decreasing salt concentration. 

Option C: The organic solvent formamide, which is commonly used in recombinant DNA experiments, destabilizes hydrogen bonding between bases, thereby lowering the Tm. Formamide addition allows the strands of DNA or DNA–RNA hybrids to be separated at much lower temperatures and minimizes the phosphodiester bond breakage and chemical damage to nucleotides that can occur upon extended incubation at higher temperatures.

Option D: DNA can be denatured at extreme of pH (not at physiological pH around 7.4)

Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32nd edition CH 34 PN 340

question_text: Which of the following employs CRISPR-Cas9 technology?
explanation:
Explanation:

CRISPR-Cas9 technology is used for editing specific parts of the genome by removing, adding, or altering sections of the DNA sequence. It is currently the simplest, most versatile, and precise method for genetic manipulation.

The term CRISPR stands for:

  • Clustered
  • Regulatory
  • Interspaced
  • Short
  • Palindromic
  • Repeats

The CRISPR-Cas9 system uses two main DNA repair mechanisms: Non-Homologous End Joining (NHEJ) and Homology-Directed Repair (HDR). It is a powerful tool for creating precise double-stranded breaks in DNA.

CRISPR-Cas9 System Components:

  • Guide RNA (gRNA): Directs the Cas9 enzyme to the specific DNA sequence to be edited.
  • Cas9 Enzyme: Creates double-stranded breaks at the targeted site.

Repair Mechanisms:

  • Non-Homologous End Joining (NHEJ): Joins broken DNA ends without a template, often causing small insertions or deletions. This can disrupt genes, resulting in gene knockout.
  • Homology-Directed Repair (HDR): Uses a homologous DNA template to accurately repair double-stranded breaks, enabling precise gene correction or insertion.

Explanation for other options:

Post-transcriptional Modification (Option B): This refers to the alterations made to RNA after transcription, such as splicing, capping, and polyadenylation. It does not involve CRISPR-Cas9, which primarily targets DNA rather than RNA.

DNA Induction (Option C): This term is not commonly associated with CRISPR-Cas9 technology. CRISPR-Cas9 focuses on directly editing DNA sequences rather than inducing changes.

DNA Editing Solution (Option D): Although CRISPR-Cas9 is a powerful DNA-editing tool, the phrase "DNA Editing Solution" is broad and not specifically linked to the CRISPR-Cas9 system.

Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8215069/
